title: Ang 91–93: the Bhagats of Sri Rag
hookLine: Kabir, Trilochan, Beni and Ravidas close the raga
tomorrow: who would you give everything to meet?

cards: A new person starts at work or school, and by lunch they've got a nickname, based on where they're from, before anyone has heard them say a full sentence. It happens fast.
So who gets the last word in the Granth's first raga? Not a Guru. Sri Rag closes with voices from outside the Gurus' line, and the Gurus put them there.

teach.h: THE BHAGATS: SET IN BY THE GURUS.
teach.b: From ang 91 to 93, Sri Rag ends with the bhagats: devotees whose hymns the Gurus set into the Granth beside their own.
Kabir, Trilochan, Beni, Ravidas. Tradition remembers them coming from different places and trades: Kabir a weaver, Ravidas from leatherworkers, a community looked down on in his day. Listen to them.

Kabir, on ang 91, in paraphrase: a mother watches her son grow and thinks he's getting bigger; she doesn't see that every day his life is getting shorter. It's the four watches again, in a mother's kitchen.
Ravidas, on ang 93, in paraphrase: between you and me, me and you, what difference is there?
Like gold and the bracelet made of it. Like water and the wave. Two voices from outside the Gurus' line, and the Gurus kept every word.
So what does this give you for a week like this one? A habit of attention. The Granth doesn't decide whose words count by where someone comes from.

teach.h: WORDS COUNT BY WHAT THEY CARRY.
teach.b: It decides by what the words carry.
In a gurdwara these hymns are sung and bowed to the same as the Gurus' own. The new person at the table might be the one about to say the true thing.

how: The bhagats' hymns are read and sung in the gurdwara with the same honor as the Gurus' own; each is headed with the bhagat's name, so a reader always knows whose voice it is.

o: the page where the Granth's second raga begins
the page where the bhagats' hymns start closing Sri Rag
the ninety-first hymn of Guru Nanak's morning prayer

games.q: the voices that close Sri Rag — tap the pairs.
p: devotees whose hymns the Gurus set in
the son grows; his days grow shorter
gold and the bracelet, water and wave
where the bhagats close Sri Rag

s: the Guru Granth Sahib holds only the Gurus' own hymns
the bhagats' hymns are in it too, set there by the Gurus; they close Sri Rag.
Ravidas pictures God and the soul as gold and a bracelet
and as water and its wave: between you and me, what difference?

games.q: your group project has one quiet member everyone forgets to ask. the deadline is tomorrow and the loud ones want to just finish it. what does the end of Sri Rag suggest?
o: split her part among the rest; it's faster and kinder to her.
ask her first; the raga's last word goes to voices from outside the line.
let the loudest members decide; they've earned it by doing more.
games.why: the Gurus gave the first raga's closing pages to the bhagats. whose words count isn't set by who's loudest or most familiar.

practice: If you can, read Ravidas on ang 93 first, gold and bracelet. Bring to mind one person whose voice gets less room than it should, at school, at work, at the dinner table.
Picture what you'd wish for them, what stands in the way, and one small way you could hand them the floor. Then let the plan rest, and sit with Ravidas's picture: water, and the wave.
